**My thinking:**

I've been farming this land since I was young, watching my father do the same. In Quzhou, everybody grows wheat in winter and maize in summer — that's just what the land is for. I'm not going to change that. I have about 8 mu of flat dryland that I cultivate every year on the same rotation.

For wheat, I already know I'll plant around October after the maize comes off. I use the improved variety from the county seed station — the one most of my neighbors use, something like 科农199 or similar. It gives good yield and the seed station people say it handles the dry spells okay. I put down a full bag of compound fertilizer as base, then top-dress with urea in spring at jointing. I irrigate before sowing, once in winter to protect against freeze, again at jointing, and once more at heading. That's four times. My father used to do it this way and I do too.

For maize in summer, I plant right after wheat harvest in June — no time to waste. I buy a hybrid packet every year, usually 先玉335 or whatever the village seed shop has. I throw down some compound fertilizer at planting and add urea when it's about knee-high. I don't irrigate much for maize because the summer rains usually help, but I'll do it once if it gets dry. I spray for corn borer once, sometimes twice if I see damage.

I use rotary tillage before wheat planting. For maize I just seed directly into the stubble — saves time and fuel.

I know the extension office says I'm using too much nitrogen, but I'd rather put a bit more than risk a poor harvest. I have family to feed and loans to repay.
